l: Aornos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Aornos is a strongly fortified rock and refuge, about one hundred furlongs around and sixteen high, above the Indus. Guided by an old man, Alexander blocked its only passage, raised a mount, and drove defenders to abandon it at night.

l: Indus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Indus is a river, described as the greatest river of India, running at the southern foot of Aornos. Alexander reached it, built a bridge with thirty-oared ships, rested his army for thirty days, and offered sacrifices. Hephaestion and Perdiccas were sent ahead to prepare its crossing with Taxiles and other commanders. As Alexander’s forces and fleet moved along and down the river, neighboring peoples appeared on its banks and Sambus crossed it with elephants. Its meeting waters created dangerous whirlpools, catching Alexander’s ship before the campaign reached the main ocean.

l: Taxiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Taxiles is presented chiefly as an Indian petty prince and former king beyond the Indus, later called Alexander’s constant, faithful friend and associate. He came with other princes, gave Indian presents, promised twenty-five elephants, accompanied commanders into Peucelaotis, and helped Alexander trust Sangius. The records also call Taxiles the province where Alexander refreshed his army before Porus; after his death Mophis succeeded him and was called Taxiles.

l: Mophis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Mophis, Taxiles’ son and successor, offered Alexander assistance and his kingdom, approached with army and elephants, then surrendered himself and forces after suspicion; Alexander restored his kingdom.

l: Alexandrian campaign in India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Indian campaign in which Alexander pursued Massaga mercenaries, took cities and Aornos, crossed the Indus, received forces and elephants, and allied with and restored Mophis.

l: massacre of the Massaga mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: After the Massaga mercenaries had been allowed to leave their city, Alexander pursued and attacked them without warning. The mercenaries and their wives resisted in a circular formation but were overwhelmed, and the unarmed survivors and remaining women were distributed among Alexander's horsemen.

l: siege and capture of Aornos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander learned the approaches to Aornos from an old man who lived nearby, seized the only passage to the summit, and built a mount toward the fort. After seven days of continuous assault, he withdrew the guard blocking the passage, and the defenders fled by night, leaving Alexander in possession of the rock.

l: Mophis's submission to Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a submission [Mophis delivered himself and his army to Alexander] Mophis approached Alexander with a well-equipped army and elephants after previously promising assistance and the surrender of his kingdom. Although Alexander first suspected an attack, Mophis halted his forces and surrendered himself and his army; Alexander rewarded the submission by restoring him to his kingdom.

l: Roxana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Roxana, daughter of Oxyartes and Gayares, was judged among Asia’s most beautiful women and married Alexander. She became mother of Alexander IV. After Alexander’s affairs, Cassander imprisoned Roxana and her son at Amphipolis to destroy Alexander’s posterity, then ordered Glaucias to murder them; Roxana was killed and her body concealed.

l: Porus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Porus, a prince commanding an Indian army and allied with Embisarus, fought Alexander with strength and courage, was wounded, fell from his elephant, and was captured. After recovering, he was restored to his kingdom.

l: Embisarus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Embisarus, a neighboring king as powerful as Porus, delayed aid, feared the battle, and was compelled by Alexander to submit.

l: Publius Cornelius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Publius Cornelius is a Roman consul, influenced by philosophy in truth as well as words. Renowned for virtue, birth, piety, prudence, and judgment, he is judged Rome’s best citizen and urges preserving Carthage to restrain pride and maintain peace.

l: Calanus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Calanus, an Indian philosopher honored by Alexander, remained healthy until illness at seventy-three; after sailing with familiar friends, he sought permission to die on a funeral pile, was consumed by fire, and honorably buried.

l: Coragus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Coragus is a strong Macedonian soldier, reputed for gallantry, who challenges Dioxippus to a duel but is defeated, knocked down, and released on Alexander’s order.

l: Dioxippus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Dioxippus is an Athenian Greek champion, stronger than Coragus and a winner of many prizes and victories. He defeats the Macedonian Coragus in single combat by breaking his sarissa and knocking him down. Later falsely accused of stealing a golden cup, he writes to Alexander and commits suicide.

l: India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: India is a region of neighboring kingdoms ruled by Porus and Embisarus, and home to Ceteus and his soldiers. After leaving Bactria, Alexander advanced toward and through it, passing between Cophen and Indus and intending its utmost bounds and the ocean. It is marked by accounts of marriage, poisoning, widow-burning, Bacchus's conquest, and the Nysaeans' claim of ivy at Nysa.

l: Hydaspes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Hydaspes is a fierce river, seven furlongs wide and six fathoms deep, near a battlefield. Alexander’s forces crossed it; after moving toward it from Phigeus, he built one city beyond the crossing and another where he overcame Porus.

l: Ganges, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Ganges was reported to lie beyond a twelve-day desert and to be twenty-two furlongs wide and the deepest river in India. The Gandarites were said to dwell beyond it.

l: Gedrosia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Gedrosia contains rude, savage whale-eating people and a barren, provisionless wilderness; Alexander marches through it, brings its inhabitants to submission easily, then follows the sea-coast through savage peoples and wilderness.

l: battle of Alexander and Porus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Battle involving Alexander and Porus: Alexander's horse broke Indian chariots, elephants hurt Macedonians, then panicked and trampled Indians; Porus charged with forty elephants before being overcome.

l: Alexander's victory over Porus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander’s victory causes Indian flight and heavy losses; he takes prisoners and elephants, sacrifices to the sun, and restores wounded Porus’s kingdom.

l: Alexander's crossing of the Hydaspes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander crossed the river Hydaspes with his forces. He built a city on the farther side of the river at the crossing and another at the place where he defeated Porus.

l: elephants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Elephants, positioned like towers before Porus’s army, initially crushed Macedonians but, struck by darts, panicked, broke formation, and trampled their own soldiers.

l: Indian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Indian army under Porus fielded more than fifty thousand foot soldiers, three thousand horse, over a thousand chariots, and 130 elephants; it lost over twelve thousand and had over nine thousand captured.

l: Porus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a friend of Alexander Porus received the kingdom of the neighboring prince after Hephastion subdued it for Alexander. Alexander later questioned Porus about the reported strength of the Gandarites, and Porus confirmed the report.

l: Gandarites, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Gandarites were reported to live beyond the Ganges and to be ruled by Xandrames. Their king was said to command twenty thousand horse, two hundred thousand foot, two thousand chariots, and four thousand elephants.

l: Sopithes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Sopithes is a king, notably tall, who rules a kingdom and law-governed cities valuing beauty, health, and strength. He submits to Alexander, regains his kingdom, entertains the army, and gives 150 powerful tiger-dog hybrids.

l: Oxydracee, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a populous and warlike nation [in India] The Oxydracee were a populous and warlike Indian nation that joined with the Mallii against Alexander. Their capital city was besieged and captured after Alexander was wounded during the assault.

l: Mallii, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a populous and warlike nation [in India] The Mallii were a populous and warlike Indian nation that confederated with the Oxydracee against Alexander. Their capital city was assaulted and taken, after which the Macedonians killed the men they found there.

l: capital city of the Oxydracee and Mallii, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The capital city was targeted by Alexander without delay despite a soothsayer’s warning that he would be wounded. Alexander entered through the gate, climbed the wall, was left isolated when the ladders broke, and was struck by a severe wound before being rescued.

l: soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: use Indian plaids [cut into pieces to make clothing] The soldiers were described as exhausted and poorly equipped after years of campaigning. Their wives and children were gathered by Alexander, and corn was ordered to be distributed monthly among the wives.

l: marriage customs of the Cathari, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The records describe an Indian widow-burning law: after wives allegedly poisoned husbands, it required a widow’s self-immolation with her deceased husband. Pregnant widows and those who had borne children were excepted. A widow who refused remained a widow and lost sacred rites and legal privileges. The law is characterized as cruel and inhuman.

l: the Indian widow's self-immolation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: occurs_at the funeral pyre [after the funeral of Ceteus] The younger of Ceteus's two wives voluntarily burned herself with his body after being judged eligible under the Indian custom. She gave her ornaments to servants and friends, took leave of her family, and died with what the spectators regarded as heroic courage.

l: conquest of India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The conquest continued through the submission or capture of numerous Indian territories and cities. Hephastion was praised after subduing a great part of India, while Alexander continued toward the Oxydracee and Mallii.

l: invasion of the Gandarites, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_difficult military expedition [as perceived by Alexander] Alexander wished to invade the Gandarites after hearing of their powerful army beyond the Ganges. He recognized the expedition’s difficulty but initially intended to proceed, although his soldiers’ exhaustion and poor condition threatened the plan.

l: duel between Coragus and Dioxippus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A public single combat between Coragus and Dioxippus, won by Dioxippus. Coragus fought armed, while Dioxippus fought naked with a club; Dioxippus avoided the javelin, broke the sarissa, stopped Coragus drawing his sword, and knocked him down. Alexander then ordered Coragus released.

l: Dioxippus's suicide, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Dioxippus’s suicide followed a false theft accusation after courtiers planted a golden cup under his cushion. He wrote to Alexander protesting that his enemies had plotted against him, entrusted the letter to servants, and killed himself. Alexander was greatly troubled, later regretted the death, and recognized Dioxippus’s honesty and the accusers’ knavery.

l: river voyage and shipwrecks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: includes shipwrecks [at the meeting of the rivers and the Indus] Alexander and his companions sailed down the rivers toward their confluence, where violent whirlpools destroyed or damaged several vessels. Two long ships sank, others were driven ashore, and Alexander’s own ship was caught before he was brought safely to land.

l: siege of the Oxydracee and Mallii capital, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: causes Alexander's wounding [Alexander is wounded under one breast] Alexander ordered an immediate assault on the capital despite Demophoon’s warning. The Macedonian ladders broke when too many men climbed them, leaving Alexander isolated on the wall until Peucestes and other guards reached him.

l: Alexander's wounding, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_inflicted_during siege of the Oxydracee and Mallii capital [by an Indian] During the assault on the capital, Alexander received many blows on his helmet and shield and was finally wounded beneath one breast. He killed the Indian who had wounded him, remained standing with the aid of a tree, and was eventually rescued.

l: Oxydracee and Mallii army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: has_size above eighty thousand foot, ten thousand horse, and seven hundred chariots The Oxydracee and Mallii were prepared with an army of more than eighty thousand foot, ten thousand horse, and seven hundred chariots. Instead of confronting Alexander in the open field, their forces withdrew into neighboring cities after disputes over supreme command.

l: Sogdiana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander's forces entered Sogdiana and reduced the cities that had revolted. The Sogdians later used a rock in Sogdiana as a refuge.

l: Dioxippus's false theft accusation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Dioxippus is framed when the king’s friends and courtiers plant a golden cup under his cushion during a feast, accuse him of theft, supposedly find it there, disgrace him, and drive him from the table.

l: Brachmanes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Brachmanes, inhabitants of Harmatelia, revolted after submitting; during Alexander's campaigns, many people in their territories were destroyed or enslaved, over eighty thousand barbarians were killed, and most submitters were pardoned.

l: Harmatelia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Harmatelia, a strong, well-fenced city, was the last city attacked among the Brachmanes; trusting its valor and position, its inhabitants ultimately begged Alexander’s pardon and surrendered themselves and their city.

l: siege of Harmatelia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Before the siege, Alexander used a feigned retreat to draw three thousand inhabitants of Harmatelia into battle. The defenders used deadly snake poison on their weapons, causing severe suffering and death among the wounded, but the inhabitants later surrendered when Alexander began the siege.

l: Ptolemy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Ptolemy is presented chiefly as a Macedonian commander who becomes king and ruler of Egypt. Early on, he is loved for valor and obliging behavior after Alexander heals a poisoned wound. After the division of provinces, he takes Egypt, governs it mildly, uses a treasury of eight thousand talents to hire mercenaries, allies with Antipater against Perdiccas, and gains Cyrene through Ophelas. He honors Alexander by receiving the body in Syria, keeping it in Alexandria, and establishing a temple, sacrifices, and magnificent rites. His power rests on Egypt, strong garrisons, wealth, fleets, armies, and support won through loyalty and affection. He defends Egypt against Perdiccas, treats enemy dead honorably, and declines a higher protectorship. He expands into Syria, Phoenicia, Coele-Syria, Cyprus, Cilicia, and Greek cities, while repeatedly aligning with or opposing Antipater, Cassander, Seleucus, Lysimachus, Antigonus, Demetrius, and Eumenes. He defeats Demetrius at Gaza, yet later withdraws to Egypt, destroying or abandoning Syrian and Phoenician positions when Antigonus approaches. The record emphasizes both force and calculated generosity: he rewards commanders, releases prisoners, returns Demetrius's dead and household without ransom, aids Rhodes with supplies and soldiers, and is later worshipped there as a god. He also suffers major reverses, notably defeat by Demetrius at sea near Salamis, after which he assumes the title of king. He fortifies the Nile and preserves Egypt against invasion, later joins leagues against Antigonus, and returns from a truce at Sidon after a false report. The final material also portrays a Ptolemy who loses Egypt, is blamed for surrendering it without a struggle, is expelled, and travels toward Rome.

l: Ptolemy's healing, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: uses healing herb [as poultice and potion] Alexander dreamed that a serpent showed him an herb and explained its nature and location. He found the herb, applied it as a poultice, and gave Ptolemy its juice as a potion, curing Ptolemy and later other wounded men.

l: Hyala, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a city [famous city at the river's mouth] Hyala was a famous city governed like Lacedaemon, with two hereditary kings responsible for war and a senate holding chief authority in civil affairs. Alexander reached it after returning up the river, repaired or burned his defective ships there, and entrusted the remaining fleet to Nearchus and others.

l: Alexander's fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: contains leaky and defective ships [ships were beached at Hyala] Alexander's fleet sailed into the main ocean and reached two islands where magnificent sacrifices were offered. At Hyala, defective ships were burned, while the remaining ships were placed under Nearchus and other friends to explore the sea-coast to the entrance of the river Euphrates.

l: desert crossing, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: During the desert crossing, Alexander's army passed through waterless tracts and a wilderness lacking all support for human life. Many soldiers died from hunger, and mountaineers later attacked Leonatus's squadron, causing another loss.

l: sea-coast exploration, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: reports tides of the ocean [large islands appeared at low water and were submerged at high tide] Nearchus and other friends were ordered to sail along the sea-coast, observe every place carefully, and continue to the entrance of the river Euphrates. They later reported extraordinary tides, submerged islands, fierce winds, and whales of incredible size.

l: Calanus's self-immolation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: uses funeral pile [Calanus ascended it and was consumed] Calanus's self-immolation occurred when he ascended a funeral pile and was burned with it, following his own philosophical convictions. Some witnesses judged the act madness or vanity, while others admired his courage and contempt for death.

l: Alexander's funeral pile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander built Hephaestion’s funeral pile at Babylon after removing bricks from ten furlongs of city wall. The foursquare structure measured one furlong on each side, contained thirty apartments and decorated levels, and rose more than one hundred and thirty cubits.

l: thirty thousand Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: are_armed_with Macedonian arms [fully equipped] Thirty thousand young Persian men, trained in martial discipline and equipped with Macedonian arms, came to Susa. They demonstrated their skill before Alexander and received large and rich gifts; Alexander intended them to serve as a curb upon the Macedonian phalanx.

l: Tenarus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_in Laconia Tenarus in Laconia was the place where discharged mercenary soldiers gathered. Persian governors and commanders brought additional men and money there, and the combined forces appointed Leosthenes as their general.

l: Thimbron, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: commands army of mercenaries [after taking Harpalus's soldiers] Thimbron took Harpalus's money, soldiers, and navy, then invaded the country of the Cyrenians with the aid of Cyrenian exiles. Although he won several engagements and besieged Cyrene, he suffered reverses, was defeated by Ophelas, and was captured.

l: Macedonian mutiny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_caused_by Macedonians [their insolence and opposition to Alexander] The Macedonian mutiny grew from the soldiers' opposition to Alexander and their resentment of Persian appointments to chief commands. Alexander seized some leaders and delivered them to the lictors for execution, after which the Macedonians sought reconciliation through petitions and tears.

l: Peucestes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Peucestes is a Persian governor and general, formerly Alexander's bodyguard, who governs most of Persia and is greatly beloved by its natives. Chosen unanimously to command a Macedonian army assembled from provincial forces, he brings large numbers of Persian darters, slingers, archers, infantry, and cavalry. After initially withholding archers because he lacks chief command, he supplies ten thousand, distributes booty, and holds a feast at Persepolis, arousing Eumenes's suspicion; Eumenes first weakens and then reconciles with him. Fearing Antigonus, Peucestes flees a battle and refuses to fight again, contributing to Eumenes's defeat. Antigonus later removes him from Persia through false hopes of higher preferment despite native opposition.

l: Lamian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Lamian War was a war between the Athenians and Antipater, begun after Alexander’s death amid the gathering of discharged mercenaries under Leosthenes. Greek forces initially defeated the Macedonians and besieged Lamia, but Antipater and Craterus later defeated them, broke their confederacy, forced separate negotiations, and ended the war with Athenian submission.

l: mercenary soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: assemble_at Tenarus [after being discharged and lacking subsistence] After being discharged under the king's order, many mercenary soldiers wandered through Asia without subsistence and robbed and spoiled the country. They eventually gathered together at Tenarus in Laconia.

l: Cussaei, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cussaei were a warlike nation in Media's mountains, never subdued during the Persian empire. Alexander repeatedly defeated and captured many of them, ending their resistance by compelling loyalty and obedience.

l: Cussae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander first seized the passes into the country of Cussae and ravaged much of it. After overcoming its defenders and taking many prisoners, he built cities at the most difficult passes before marching away.

l: conquest of the Cussaei, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: lasts forty days [Alexander's conquest] Alexander's conquest of the Cussaei lasted forty days. He secured the passes, defeated the inhabitants, forced them to surrender their liberty for the preservation of their country, and established cities at difficult points.

l: astrology, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: uses stars [to prognosticate future events] The Chaldeans used astrology to prognosticate future events by observing the stars. Their astrologers predicted Alexander's death after entering Babylon, but philosophical arguments persuaded him to despise divination, especially that of the Chaldeans.

l: Hephaestion's funeral, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: receives_honours tutelary god [Alexander commanded all to sacrifice to Hephaestion as a tutelar god] Alexander arranged Hephaestion’s funeral with greater pomp than any earlier funeral and intended it never to be surpassed. Commanders, soldiers, ambassadors, and inhabitants contributed to it, and its cost exceeded twelve thousand talents.

l: Alexander's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander’s death, foretold by prodigies, followed a violent illness after he drank at a banquet from Hercules’s cup. Dying without issue, he predicted contention among commanders over his funeral; his death left government leaderless, triggered succession disputes and revolt, and ended proposed projects.

l: ambassadors to Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: come_from all parts of the world [almost all parts] Ambassadors came to Alexander from almost every part of the world. They came to congratulate him, offer crowns and gifts, make leagues and alliances, clear themselves of accusations, or oppose the restoration of exiles; Alexander arranged the order in which they would be received.

l: Craterus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Craterus was a Macedonian commander renowned for good conduct. He led soldiers in Cilicia, commanded the siege of Cyropolis, where he was wounded, and later arrived from Cilicia with reinforcements for Antipater, taking chief command of their combined army. He helped defeat the Greeks, besiege Thessalian cities, establish peace, married Phila, campaigned against the Aetolians, and commanded forces jointly with Antipater. Opposed by Eumenes at the Hellespont, he led the force against him and the right wing in battle. Thrown from his horse, he was trampled unrecognized and killed.

l: Sysigambis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Sysigambis, the mother of Darius, mourned Alexander’s death with many tears and refused both food and light. She died of hunger on the fifth day, in extreme sorrow but with honor and reputation.

l: Alexander's illness, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander’s fatal illness began after heavy drinking at Medius’s banquet, worsened into severe pain beyond physicians’ relief, led to despair and giving his ring to Perdiccas, and ended in death.

l: Alexander's poisoning theory, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Some writers claimed that Alexander died from a deadly potion rather than from illness. They attributed the alleged poisoning to Antipater, who supposedly ordered his cup-bearer son to put poison in Alexander’s wine, although the account notes that some historians may have avoided reporting this because of Antipater’s power and Cassander’s succession.

l: prodigies foretelling Alexander's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The extinguishing of the Persian Holy Fire during Hephaestion’s funeral was regarded as an omen of Alexander’s death. Other prodigies included a chained man putting on Alexander’s robes and crown and sitting on his throne, and Alexander’s diadem being lost in the water and later recovered by a sailor; diviners interpreted these events as warnings and advised sacrifices.

l: Aridaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Aridaeus, Philip’s son, was described as weak-spirited and naturally infirm. After Alexander’s death he was made king, later named Philip III. He spent two years preparing Alexander’s funeral chariot and transported Alexander’s body from Babylon toward Egypt. He held sovereign authority as protector of the kings, came from the Nile to Triparadisus with the kings and army, and was Eurydice’s husband. As governor of Phrygia at the Hellespont, he fortified cities and unsuccessfully besieged Cyzicum. Defying Antigonus, he later fled to a city of the Ganians, joined Clitus, and strengthened his army.

l: king Philip, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Philip III, the name given to Aridaeus, was made king after Alexander’s death and reigned six years and four months. He summoned commanders while Perdiccas held executive power, was husband of Eurydice, and later joined other kings under Eumenes. After Macedonians abandoned Eurydice, Olympias imprisoned Philip and had Thracians stab him to death.

l: Seleucus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Seleucus is a Macedonian commander, governor, prince of the higher provinces, and later king whose career centers on Babylon, conflict with Antigonus, and alliances with other rulers. While governor of provinces centered on Babylon and lord-lieutenant of Susa, he refused to obey Eumenes, attempted to win Antigenes and the Argyraspides, flooded Eumenes’s camp by diverting the Tigris, made a truce for Eumenes’s crossing, and informed Antigonus. When Antigonus came to Babylon and demanded an accounting of its revenues, Seleucus claimed the province had been granted for his service under Alexander. Fearful of Antigonus, he fled with fifty horsemen to Egypt, where Ptolemy received and supported him. From this exile he opposed Antigonus through Ptolemy. He commanded operations in Cyprus through Polyclitus, with Menelaus and allied forces, taking Cyrinia and Lapithus, gaining Stasiecus, demanding hostages, and besieging Citium. He persuaded Ptolemy to invade Coele-Syria, joined Ptolemy against Demetrius, and presented their struggle as a response to Antigonus’s seizure of conquered provinces and deprivation of Babylon. After Demetrius’s defeat at Gaza, Seleucus returned toward Babylon with only eight hundred infantry and two hundred cavalry, trusting the inhabitants’ affection. With their support he recovered Babylon, defeated Nicanor near the Tigris, secured Media, Susa, and neighboring provinces, and later prospered in the upper provinces. He appointed Patrocles over Babylon and responded when Demetrius again threatened it. Seleucus then joined Cassander, Ptolemy, and Lysimachus against Antigonus, raised a numerous army, and marched from Babylon with a great force. In Cappadocia he wintered with 20,000 foot, 12,000 horse, 480 elephants, and 100 iron chariots before joining Lysimachus for war. He also rejected a request to kill the imprisoned Demetrius, sought his son Antiochus Soter’s advice, and intended to release Demetrius honorably. He is recorded as Antiochus’s father and as bound through his father’s league with Rome.

l: Antiphilus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: succeeds Leosthenes [as general] Antiphilus was described as a prudent and valiant commander. He was appointed general in place of Leosthenes after Leosthenes died.

l: Greeks in the upper provinces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Greeks in the upper provinces, a revolting population, endured remote settlement under Alexander. After his death they sought to return to Greece, chose Python, raised over twenty thousand infantry and three thousand cavalry, were defeated, and ultimately killed by Macedonians.

l: Alexander's captains, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander's captains were commanders and bodyguards who participated in settling the succession. Under the authority of the king and Perdiccas, they were assigned responsibility for governing provinces and regions, while former lieutenant-governors in Asia retained their governments. Their distribution begins with appointments across Egypt, Asia, and neighboring provinces, including military command for Seleucus, and extends through Persia, Media, Babylon, Mesopotamia, Thrace, Macedonia, and other regions.

l: Greek revolt in the upper provinces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_caused_by desire to return to Greece [following Alexander's death] The Greek revolt in the upper provinces began after Alexander's death, when the Greeks sought to escape their exile and return to Greece. Perdiccas sent Python against it with Macedonian troops and reinforcements from the provincial governors; the revolt was defeated, and its participants were killed.

l: succession crisis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The succession crisis followed Alexander's death without issue. The infantry supported Aridaeus, while leading nobles, bodyguards, and the Social Horse prepared to oppose the Macedonian phalanx; the dispute was settled by making Aridaeus king as Philip III and Perdiccas executive authority.

l: division of the provinces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The division of the provinces placed Egypt under Ptolemy, Syria under Laomedon, Cilicia under Philotas, Media under Pithon, Cappadocia and Paphlagonia under Eumenes, Lycia and Greater Phrygia under Antigonus, Caria under Cassander, Lydia under Meleager, and other territories under various commanders. Macedonia and the neighboring regions were assigned to Antipater, while Lysimachus received Thrace and the areas bordering the Pontus.

l: Tanais, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Tanais is the improperly used name for the Iaxartes, a river reached by Asiatic Scythians; it is explicitly distinguished from the Tanais flowing into Lake Maeotis.

l: Lamia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Lamia became Antipater’s refuge after his defeat. He strengthened its walls and accumulated arms, grain, and other provisions there while the Macedonian army waited for reinforcements. Lamia was under siege when the Greeks withdrew to meet Leonatus. Antipater had previously been shut up there, and Athens later surrendered after the Macedonian victory.

l: Greek exiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: More than twenty thousand Greek exiles gathered at the Olympiads when Alexander’s restoration order was proclaimed. Their restoration was welcomed by many, but opposed by the Aetolians and Athenians.

l: Alexander’s restoration letter, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander’s restoration letter addresses Greek exiles, denying responsibility for their banishment and promising their return to their own countries except for those banished for outrageous crimes. It concludes by ordering Antipater to use force against opponents of the restoration.

l: Aetolians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Aetolians were a people of Aetolia described as warrior people, with ten thousand brave and sprightly men and mountain strongholds. They opposed Alexander’s recall of exiles, expecting to punish Oenians expelled from Aetolia, then supplied Leosthenes with seven thousand soldiers and joined the Greek confederacy before public concerns drew them home. Resisting Antipater and Craterus, they held difficult passes and fortified cities, repelled initial attacks, but winter hardship led to a temporary peace after Antigonos disclosed Perdiccas’s plans. They later campaigned in Thessaly under Alexander, besieging Amphissa, ravaging Locrian territory, defeating Polycles, and then withdrawing forces when Acarnanians invaded Aetolia. They supported Antigonus against Cassander, fought Acarnanians, and killed surrendering people at Agrinium despite safe conduct. After Philip defeated their allies and killed Aecidas, they fled with their families to mountain strongholds. Finally, their peace envoys faced Rome’s demand to surrender their country or pay one thousand talents; appeals based on services to Rome failed.

l: Alexander’s order recalling the exiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: causes Athenians [to wait for an opportunity to act] Alexander’s order required the Greek cities to receive their exiles, with an exception for those banished for outrageous crimes. The order angered the Aetolians and Athenians, who had different interests in the exiles and their property.

l: Harpalus’s treasure, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a vast treasure [left by Harpalus] Harpalus’s treasure provided financial support for the Lamian War. Athens sent part of it to Leosthenes, who distributed the money among the soldiers and used it to arm those who lacked weapons.

l: Athens’s war decree, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Athens’s war decree assigns Athenians the defense of Greece’s common liberty and the freeing of Greek cities from garrisons. It then calls for forty three-banked and two hundred four-banked ships, mobilizes Athenians under forty, and sends ambassadors to Greek cities.

l: Greek confederacy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Greek confederacy formed after Athenian ambassadors won support for war, uniting Aetolians, most Thessalians, Thebans, and Peloponnesian communities, while some Greeks backed Macedonians or remained neutral.

l: Pyllene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a fortified camp [Leosthenes blocked the passages there] After defeating the Boeotians, Leosthenes returned to Pyllene. He blocked the passages there and encamped while awaiting the Macedonian army.

l: Crat erus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: commands Macedonian army [thirty thousand Macedonians in Cilicia] Crat erus was in Cilicia with thirty thousand Macedonians who had been dismissed from service in Asia. Antipater summoned him to come with all available forces to assist against the Greek uprising.

l: Battle of the Lamian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: ends_in Macedonian defeat [the Grecians overcame the Macedonians] In a battle of the Lamian War, the Greeks overpowered and defeated the Macedonians. Antipater then fled to Lamia rather than remain in the field or return to Macedonia.

l: siege of Lamia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The siege of Lamia was a blockade conducted by Leosthenes against Antipater's Macedonian army. Leosthenes enclosed Lamia with fortifications to cut off supplies, but Macedonian resistance and Antipater's sally fatally injured him. The Greeks then abandoned the siege when Leonatus approached to relieve Antipater.

l: Leosthenes’s death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Leosthenes’s death followed a stone blow to the head during Antipater’s sally. Carried half dead into camp, he died three days later and was honorably buried for his services in the war.

l: Hyperides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: delivers funeral oration for Leosthenes [at the Athenians' command] Hyperides was ordered by the Athenians to deliver Leosthenes’s funeral oration. He was regarded as the foremost orator of the time for his eloquence and his particular hatred of the Macedonians.

l: Macedonian yoke, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Leosthenes urged the neighboring nations to free Greece from the Macedonian yoke. Athens likewise presented its war against the Macedonians as a struggle for the common liberty of Greece.

l: Greek cities’ garrisons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Athens’s war decree called for all Greek cities to be freed from their several garrisons. The decree made removing these garrisons part of Athens’s stated defense of Greek liberty.

l: Alexander’s Asian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The soldiers dismissed by the governors of Asia included experienced men who had fought in many major battles. Eight thousand of them were near Taenarus and were secretly recruited by Leosthenes, while thirty thousand more were with Craterus in Cilicia.

l: Lysimachus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Lysimachus is a king and military ruler whose career centers on Thrace, repeated wars, shifting alliances, and expansion into Asia. He begins as a fighter close to Alexander: he killed a lion in Syria with his own hand, suffered a left shoulder torn to the bone, and was later restrained from attacking another lion with Alexander’s hunting spear. In Thrace he invaded, fought Seuthes while badly outnumbered, withdrew after heavy losses nearly victorious, and later campaigned against rebels, taking Odessus and the Istrian city, defeating Scythians, besieging Callantinians, fighting through Seuthes’s force at Mount Haemus, and killing Pausanias. He founded Lysimachia in Chersonesus and held chief command in Thrace under a peace with Cassander, Ptolemy, and Antigonus. His position remained contested: he faced revolts, lost the Callantinian garrison, was defeated while trying to relieve Antipater, and was captured by Dromichaetes, who treated him courteously and sought the return of Thracian forts and castles. Lysimachus repeatedly joined Cassander, Ptolemy, and Seleucus against Antigonus, though he also made peace with Antigonus. He entered Asia, freed Lampsacus and Paros, captured Sigeum and territory in the Hellespont and Phrygia, sent Prepelaus against Aeolia and Ionia, and avoided battle before wintering. Near Heraclea he joined Seleucus for a future campaign despite desertions to Antigonus. He also supported the Rhodians with wheat and barley and was related to Stratonice through Antiochus.

l: Clitus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Clitus, a Macedonian raised by Lanice, saved Alexander at the Granicus and credited Macedonians for many of Alexander’s achievements. He opposed Alexander’s barbarian customs, hated flatterers, and, while intoxicated, defended Philip and ancient heroes, disparaged Alexander, and was killed by him. Later, as Polyperchon’s admiral, Clitus commanded the Macedonian fleet and the Hellespont, won sea fights at the Echinades and near Byzantium, then was surprised by Antigonus, fled his ship, and was killed by Lysimachus’s soldiers.

l: Ariarathes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Ariarathes is a Cappadocian prince and king, though the records combine several rulers of that name. One resisted the Macedonian empire, was defeated, captured, scourged, and crucified by Perdiccas. Another, adopted as lawful heir, fled to Armenia, recovered Cappadocia, married Stratonice, maintained goodwill and alliance with Rome, and opposed ties with Demetrius.

l: Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Eumenes is presented as a Cardian commander, skilful and prudent general, and constant, faithful friend whose career centers on defending the kings and opposing Antigonus’s bid for the kingdom. He begins by receiving Cappadocia from Perdiccas, raising cavalry there, and marching with a strengthened army. He defeats Neoptolemus and Craterus’s army, though he is wounded and later condemned to death by Macedonians despite the victory. After further conflict, including the capture of Perdiccas and his army, Antigonus defeats him in Cappadocia; Eumenes retreats to the impregnable Nora with loyal followers, endures confinement or siege there, and is eventually released under an agreement. Restored to action, he is urged by Polyperchon to remain loyal to the kings and is made their general throughout Asia, with authority, money, and command of the Argyraspides. He gathers troops, escapes attempts on his life, seeks to recover Phoenicia, then marches through difficult territory to Persia, Babylon, Susa, and Persepolis. He secures royal funds, pays his soldiers, organizes consultations, strengthens his authority through political measures including a forged letter, and resists Antigonus through defenses, surprise attacks, false reports, and a fire-signal stratagem. Illness forces him to travel in a litter, but he continues to command allied forces supported by cavalry and elephants. His struggle ends disastrously: after fighting Antigonus and losing baggage, he is seized by Macedonians, delivered to Antigonus, and put to death. The records also credit him with gaining Abdera by bribery through Python, rewarding Gauls and soldiers generously, receiving regions on this side of Taurus from Roman commissioners, and later falling under Roman suspicion because of alleged alliance with Perseus. Across the account, his military ability, loyalty to the kings, persistence after defeat, and ultimate betrayal are the defining features.

l: Solon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Solon is an Athenian and one of the Seven Wise Men, distinguished for wisdom, learning, prudent counsel, and laws for Athens. Honored for good government, he gradually turns Athenians from luxurious manners toward virtue and honorable action.

l: Cyrenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: revolt_against Ptolemy [king of Egypt] The Cyrenians were first defeated by Thimbron and forced to agree to pay five thousand talents and provide half of their war chariots. Under Mnasiclus's influence they resisted further payments, later fought Thimbron, and eventually lost their independence when Ophelas delivered their cities to Ptolemy.

l: Mnasiclus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a captain [a Cretan-born expert commander] Mnasiclus, a Cretan captain of Thimbron, quarreled with him over the division of spoils and defected to the Cyrenians. He accused Thimbron of cruelty and breach of faith and persuaded the Cyrenians to resist him.

l: Ophelas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Ophelas, a captain of Alexander, led Ptolemy’s forces for the Cyrenian exiles, defeated and captured Thimbron, recovered the towns, and delivered Cyrene and neighboring cities to Ptolemy. He later ruled them, seeking to enlarge his dominions. Promised sovereignty of Africa, he agreed to aid his friend Agathocles against the Carthaginians and crossed a dangerous route with an army. Agathocles accused him of treachery, decoyed and killed him, and took his army.

l: war in Cyrene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The war in Cyrene began when Thimbron invaded with Harpalus's former soldiers and allied with Cyrenian exiles. After alternating successes, internal division among the Cyrenians, and Ptolemaic intervention under Ophelas, Thimbron was defeated and Cyrene became subject to Ptolemy.

l: battle against Leonatus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: In the battle against Leonatus, the Thessalian cavalry defeated the Macedonian forces before Antipater could join them. Leonatus was killed, while the Macedonian phalanx withdrew to defensible hills.

l: conquest of Cappadocia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The conquest of Cappadocia was achieved by Perdiccas after he defeated Ariarathes's army. Ariarathes and his kindred were executed, and the province was assigned to Eumenes of Cardia.

l: settlement of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: establishes Athenian democracy [under Antipater's conditions] The settlement of Athens followed the city's surrender to Antipater. The government remained a democracy but was restricted by property qualifications; poorer citizens were removed and offered settlements in Thessaly, while a garrison under Menyllos was installed.

l: Cyrenean civil conflict, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Cyrenean civil conflict arose during Thimbron's siege, when shortages caused the Cyrenians to quarrel and the poorer majority expelled the wealthy citizens. The exiles sought help from Ptolemy, whose forces under Ophelas defeated Thimbron and ended Cyrene's independence.

l: Isaurians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Isaurians, inhabitants of their city, had abundant weapons and defended liberty against Perdiccas and the Macedonians. Facing inevitable defeat, they destroyed their families, wealth, and houses, then remaining defenders chose death in the flames over surrender.

l: city of the Isaurians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A large, well-fortified city of the Isaurians, resolutely defended until many citizens fell after two days of assaults; it was burned, and silver and gold were found in its ruins.

l: Isaurian city destruction, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a destruction of a city [carried out by Perdiccas's forces] The destruction of the Isaurian city occurred when its inhabitants burned their houses, families, wealth, and themselves to avoid capture and enslavement. After the fire was extinguished, the soldiers of Perdiccas ransacked the ruins and found substantial silver and gold.

l: siege of the city of the Isaurians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: lasts three days [before the city's inhabitants destroy themselves] Perdiccas and the Macedonians assaulted the city of the Isaurians for two days but were forced to withdraw after suffering many casualties. On the third day, the defenders burned the city and its inhabitants while continuing to hold the walls until the besiegers drew off.

l: marriages of Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Perdiccas married Nicaea to retain Antipater's alliance and also married Cleopatra, seeking through her position and authority to secure the kingdom.

l: kingdom, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Perdiccas sought to obtain the kingdom by marrying Cleopatra and relying on her authority with the Macedonians. Antigonos warned Antipater and Craterus that Perdiccas intended to come into Macedonia as king and take the kingdom from them.

l: Demetrius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Demetrius, son of Antigonus, is a Macedonian military commander, admiral, king, and renowned besieger known as Poliorcetes for skill and violence in sieges. Young when Antigonus left him in Syria to oppose Ptolemy, he commanded mixed forces with elephants, infantry, cavalry, Macedonians, Lycians, and Pamphylians. Near Gaza he chose battle despite advice against facing the larger force of Ptolemy and Seleucus; his army was defeated after the loss of elephants and flight of cavalry, and he retreated with heavy losses. He subsequently recovered by surprising Celles, campaigned against the Nabataeans, and led an expedition toward Babylon. Acting on Antigonus's orders to liberate Greek cities, Demetrius sailed from Ephesos, took the Piraeus and Munychia, and restored Athens to liberty. In Cyprus he defeated Menelaus, besieged Salamis, routed Ptolemy's fleet, and, after the victory, assumed the title of king. He also commanded Antigonus's fleet in the Egyptian campaign. His greatest sustained enterprise was the siege of Rhodes. Seeking control of its harbour to stop supplies, he brought elaborate engines: Testudoes, four-story siege towers, a floating rampart, fortified boats, and archers and specialists. Storms, resistance, setbacks, and the surrender of four hundred of his men prevented success. Ordered by his father to make peace, he ratified an agreement with the Rhodians. He then returned to Greece, allied with the Aetolians, freed Chalcidians from a garrison, captured Sicyon and Corinth, restored liberty while retaining Corinth's citadel garrison, and acted in Achaia, Thessaly, and nearby cities. He made conditional peace with Cassander when recalled to Asia, recovered Ephesus, and fortified the mouth of Pontus. After Antigonus was killed, he fled to Cyprus with Stratonice and wealth. Later records portray him killing Alexander and Antipater, suppressing Boeotian rebels while pardoning most, and finally being imprisoned at Pella; Seleucus refused a proposal to kill him and considered restoring him to his kingdom. In war he is described as active and serious, while in peace as given to drunkenness and banqueting.

l: flight of Antigonos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a flight [from Asia to Europe] Antigonos pretended that he would defend himself against the accusations brought by Perdiccas while secretly arranging his escape. He sailed at night with his servants and his son Demetrius on ships belonging to Athens and went to Europe to join Antipater.

l: Aetolian campaign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antipater and Craterus invade Aetolia with a large army, fail to take Aetolian mountain strongholds, then secure a temporary peace after winter shortages leave the Aetolians desperate.

l: Aetolia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Aetolia, a country with cities, is invaded and spoiled by Acarnanians while the Aetolians campaign in Thessaly; the returning Aetolians drive them off. Cassander then enters to aid the Acarnanians and leaves Lyciscus with forces to continue support.

l: the army of Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Perdiccas's army was prepared for war against Ptolemy in Egypt. After Perdiccas and king Philip overcame Ariarathes, it left Pisidia toward Egypt; Perdiccas detached troops under Eumenes to secure Hellespont passes and prevent passage.

l: Perdiccas's expedition against Ptolemy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: targets Ptolemy [as its first objective] Perdiccas and his officers decided to attack Ptolemy before proceeding to Macedonia, fearing that Ptolemy would obstruct the Macedonian expedition. Perdiccas therefore marched toward Egypt while Eumenes secured the Hellespont.

l: Macedonian kings, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Macedonian kings are a royal group whose authority is exercised through commanders and protectors during campaigns and conflicts. Perdiccas plans to take them on the expedition against Ptolemy in Egypt. They later travel from the Nile to Triparadisus with Aridaeus, Python, and the army, then toward Macedonia with Antipater. After Antipater’s death, Polyperchon protects them while Antigonus seeks to disregard their authority. Acting through the kings, Polyperchon promotes peace, restored Greek governments, recalled exiles, and settlements. The kings empower Eumenes with money, troops, and full command in Asia, and remain with Polyperchon in Phocis as he seeks support in Attica and the Peloponnesus.

l: Nora, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a fort [small but impregnable] Nora was a small but impregnable fort in Cappadocia, built on a high rock and supplied with provisions for many years. Eumenes and about six hundred followers took refuge there after his defeat, and Antigonus blockaded it with walls, trenches, and earthworks.

l: Alexander's funeral chariot, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander's funeral chariot, made for Alexander's body, was exceptionally costly and magnificent, containing a golden coffin beneath a crowned roof, decorated images and achievement tables, gold-covered wheels, and sixty-four adorned mules.

l: Alexander's body, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_buried_in Alexandria [in a temple built by Ptolemy] Alexander's body was placed in a gold coffin filled partly with aromatic spices to preserve it. Aridssus brought it from Babylon toward Egypt, and Ptolemy received it in Syria and placed it in Alexandria.

l: the funeral procession, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The funeral procession attracted crowds from every city through which it passed, and spectators followed it to view the chariot. Workmen and pioneers accompanied it to level and smooth the roads.

l: the wars of the Successors, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The wars of the Successors are represented here by Perdiccas's planned war against Ptolemy in Egypt and by the effort to prevent Antipater and Craterus from crossing into Asia.

l: the army under Antipater and Craterus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: contains the phalanx [Macedonian infantry] After leaving Europe, this army was divided into two bodies: Antipater led one toward Cilicia against Perdiccas, while Craterus led the other against Eumenes. Craterus's portion was defeated in Cappadocia, and after Craterus's death and the breaking of both wings, the surviving horsemen withdrew to the phalanx.

l: Eumenes's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Eumenes's army was a force of infantry, cavalry, elephants, Argyraspides, and troops from several regions. It grew rapidly by recruitment to more than ten thousand foot and two thousand horse besides the Argyraspides and original troops, and was later reinforced by Macedonians remaining after Neoptolemus's defeat, giving it about twenty-eight thousand infantry and five thousand horse. Although Antigonus demanded Eumenes's surrender, the army remained obedient to the kings. Eumenes's sickness delayed it and discouraged the soldiers, but it marched toward Gabene and deployed about 35,000 foot, 6,100 horse, and 114 elephants. It routed Python's forces and the opposing phalanx, then suffered a reversal and refused to return to battle, choosing its carriages. In winter quarters it was dispersed, then gathered after a fire-signal stratagem and fought with 36,700 foot, 6,050 horse, and 114 elephants.

l: the battle between Eumenes and Craterus's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: In this battle, the horse on both sides advanced ahead of the infantry. Craterus was killed, Eumenes killed Neoptolemus in single combat, both enemy wings were broken, and Eumenes held the field before allowing the surviving Macedonians to depart.

l: Perdiccas's Egyptian expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: ends_in Perdiccas's death [after the failure of the crossing of the Nile] Perdiccas's expedition began with confidence after he heard of Eumenes's victory, but it was hindered by the Nile and by Ptolemy's defense of a fort. A failed river crossing caused more than two thousand deaths and turned the army and commanders against Perdiccas.

l: Perdiccas's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_caused_by the horse [the conspirators among the cavalry] Perdiccas's death occurred after his failed Egyptian operations and the Nile disaster. Disaffected commanders and soldiers conspired against him, and horsemen entered his tent and killed him; afterward, Python and Aridaeus were appointed protectors of the kings.

l: elephants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Polyperchon’s army included sixty-five elephants, whose strength was expected to break into Megalopolis. The Megalopolitans placed concealed spikes in trenches, wounding and immobilizing the elephants and causing some to trample their own troops.

l: Acarnanians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Acarnanians, at war with the Aetolians, allied with Cassander and invaded Aetolia, then followed his advice to abandon scattered forts and concentrate in stronger cities, chiefly Stratopolis.

l: Menon of Pharsalia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Menon of Pharsalia was left in Thessaly in command of the Aetolian forces. Polyperchon fought and routed him, killed him, and cut off most of his army.

l: Polyperchon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Polyperchon is a Macedonian military and political leader whose career centers on commanding armies, protecting the kings, and struggling for control of Macedonia and Greece. He first enters Thessaly with a strong army, defeats Menon’s forces, kills Menon, and recovers Thessaly. Succeeding Antipater as protector of the kings, he receives chief and absolute authority in Macedonia, invites Olympias from Epirus to act as queen-regent, and becomes Cassander’s opponent. He issues an edict restoring Greek liberties, abolishes oligarchies, promotes democratic governments, and supports Eumenes against Antigonus. During the war with Cassander, Polyperchon commands Macedonian forces, marches into Attica, and besieges Cassander at the Piraeus, while leaving his son Alexander in command of remaining troops. He tries to balance his proclaimed liberties with his wish to retain the Piraeus, and has Phocion and his followers seized. He goes into the Peloponnesus, where he restores governments in many cities but fails at Megalopolis after an elephant assault. He also assembles forces with Aeacidas, brings Olympias and Alexander’s son back into Macedonia, and employs commanders including Eumenes and Callas. His position then weakens: Callas bribes away most of his soldiers, and, after being besieged in Naxos and learning of Olympias’s death, Polyperchon flees through Thessaly with Aeacidas to Aetolia. He later holds Messenia with a garrison and remains active in the Peloponnesus. Seeking to challenge Cassander again, he supports Hercules, gathers a large army with Aetolian help, and attempts to restore Hercules to Alexander’s kingdom. Cassander persuades him to murder Hercules secretly. Polyperchon then openly joins Cassander, receives troops, withdraws into Locris after opposition, and with Cassander harasses Greece during Demetrius’s absence.

l: Triparadisus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: At Triparadisus in Higher Syria, Aridaeus and Python gave up the protectorship after conflict with Eurydice. The Macedonians then chose Antipater protector with absolute authority, and Antipater subsequently made a second division of the provinces there.

l: Eurydice, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Eurydice is a queen-regent in Macedonia and wife of Aridaeus and Philip III Arrhidaeus. She intervenes in government, seeks to control protectors, stirs Macedonians against Antipater, and claims greater fitness to rule than Olympias. She later seeks Cassander’s aid and wins supporters with bribes and promises. After Macedonians defect to Olympias, she is captured and imprisoned with Philip, tends his wounds, and kills herself with her garter when ordered to choose her death.

l: division of the provinces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: After the events at Triparadisus, Antipater made a second division of the provinces. Ptolemy retained Egypt; Laomedon received Syria; Seleucus Babylon; and Antigonus Susiana, Greater Phrygia, and Cilicia. Other commanders, including Peucestes, Python, Oxyartes, Nicanor, Cassander, Clitus, and Aridæus, received remaining provinces.

l: Oxyartes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Oxyartes, Roxana’s father, rebels against Alexander, shelters his wife and daughters in a rock refuge, and sees his young son captured after surrender.

l: royal army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antigonus was appointed general of the royal army and ordered to pursue and destroy Eumenes. The royal army was also said to be necessary for dispossessing Porus and Taxiles from their kingdoms.

l: battle in Cappadocia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antigonus and Eumenes fought a sharp battle in Cappadocia. Antigonus won after Apollonides deserted Eumenes with his horse, killed eight thousand of the enemy, and captured their baggage and carriages.

l: Coele-Syria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Coele-Syria, a region near Egypt, was sought by Ptolemy with Phoenicia for its convenient position. Nicanor brought Syria and Phoenician cities under Ptolemy's power. After Ptolemy defeated Demetrius near Gaza, he remained there, then withdrew to Egypt as Antigonus approached.

l: Aristodemus the Milesian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Aristodemus the Milesian was a general appointed by Antigonus who carried a thousand talents to the Peloponnesus, raised eight thousand soldiers, allied Antigonus with Polyperchon and Alexander, and helped install Polyperchon as general. He then commanded mercenaries against Cassander’s garrisons, relieving Cyllene, freeing Patrae, taking Aegae, and aiding Dymaea.

l: Termessus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Termessus sheltered Alcetas after his defeat. Its elders secretly betrayed him to Antigonus, while its young men resisted the betrayal, later buried Alcetas, and ravaged territory connected with Antigonus.

l: siege of Cyzicum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Aridaeus began the siege of Cyzicum with a large force and siege equipment, but the city’s defenders deceived him while preparing their defenses. Assistance from Byzantium and control of the sea enabled Cyzicum to defeat the besiegers and compel Aridaeus to withdraw; Antigonus arrived too late to relieve it.

l: battle of Alcetas in Pisidia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antigonus surprised Alcetas at Critopolis after a rapid march and seized the high ground. His larger force, cavalry, and elephants broke Alcetas’s army, captured Attalus, Docimus, Philemon, and other commanders, and drove Alcetas into Termessus.

l: death of Antipater, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The death of Antipater transferred the protection of the kings and chief authority to Polyperchon, while Cassander received the lesser office of chiliarch. News of the death contributed to disturbances and new struggles for power in Asia.

l: murder and desecration of Alcetas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alcetas was betrayed by the elders of Termessus and killed himself when their agents attacked him. Antigonus kept his body without burial for three days, then cast it out after it began to decay; the young men of Termessus recovered and buried it.

l: succession to the Macedonian regency, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antipater assigned the protection of the kings and chief authority to Polyperchon, with Cassander as chiliarch. Polyperchon then invited Olympias to return to Macedonia and act as queen-regent for Alexander’s son.

l: Antigonus's bid for sovereignty, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: includes Asia [control sought through military power and replacement of governors] Antigonus believed his army and resources made him capable of ruling Asia without regard for the kings or their guardians. He cultivated supporters, promised provinces and commands, sought Eumenes’s cooperation, challenged Aridaeus, seized royal money, and moved against provincial governors.

l: Alexander's son, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander’s young heir is placed in Olympias’s care in Macedonia until he is old enough to manage affairs alone.

l: Polypcrchon's war with Cassander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a war Polyperchon anticipated a great war with Cassander and consulted his captains and leading Macedonians about it. The proposed strategy was to weaken Cassander by restoring the cities of Greece to their liberties and abolishing oligarchies.

l: captains and commanders, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The captains and commanders took part in sacrifices before Alexander's throne and consulted there on important affairs. Eumenes maintained a respectful manner toward them and thereby avoided envy and gained their support.

l: the edict restoring Greek liberties, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The decree restores democracy, peace, and Philip’s and Alexander’s governmental order to the Greeks. It recalls exiles and restores their franchises and liberties, while excluding named groups and Megalopolis’s exiles. It restores Samos to the Athenians and assigns Polyperchon management of the decree’s matters and all other matters.

l: Philip's and Alexander's governmental order, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Philip's and Alexander's governmental order was presented as the standard to which the Greek cities would be restored. The decree granted the cities peace and authority to manage their affairs according to the rules and orders established under that order.

l: royal authority, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Royal authority was described as having been enjoyed by Antipater and as having passed into the management of others. Cassander sought to regain that sovereign authority, while Polyperchon and his allies acted in the name of the kings to preserve it.

l: Antigenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antigenes is a prudent, faithful captain and general of the Argyraspides. He commands them, resists Antigonus’s corruption and Seleucus’s and Python’s efforts to turn them against Eumenes, persuades Tautamus to abandon a plot, and argues for Eumenes and for Macedonians’ control of choosing the army’s general.

l: Macedonian captains, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: are_subject_to Eumenes [through courteous management and respect in public meetings] The Macedonian captains joined Eumenes after the kings ordered them to serve him. Eumenes treated them with equal respect and courteous language and used the ceremony of Alexander's throne to promote their unity and loyalty.

l: soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Eumenes sent trusted friends with money to recruit soldiers throughout Pisidia, Lycia, Cilicia, Coelosyria, Phoenicia, Cyprus, and other regions. More than ten thousand foot and two thousand horse were raised in addition to the Argyraspides and the troops already with him.

l: Munychia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Munychia is a naturally strong, walled fort. Nicanor held and reinforced it, repeatedly delaying a promised surrender to the Athenians; Alexander later retained it for war. It then remained with Cassander under a peace allowing him to hold it until the war with the kings ended. Governed by Dionysius and defended by a garrison, it fell to Demetrius after a sea-and-land siege and two-day assault, and was demolished.

l: throne of Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A gold throne, made from the king’s treasury after Eumenes described his dream, stood in the king’s pavilion bearing Alexander’s insignia; captains sacrificed before it and received commands in his name.

l: king's treasury, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The royal treasury at Susa supplied Eumenes with whatever money he requested under the kings' letters. He used it to pay the Macedonians six months' pay in advance and to give Eudamus two hundred talents.

l: Eumenes's appointment as general of Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a appointment [made by the kings with full and absolute authority] The kings appointed Eumenes general with full and absolute authority over Asia and ordered a thousand Macedonian Argyraspides to serve him. The appointment caused former enemies and Macedonians to accept him as their commander.

l: Antigonus's plot against Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a plot [intended to kill Eumenes through bribery and conspiracy] Antigonus sent Phiiotas, thirty Macedonians, and letters offering rewards to persuade Tautamus, Antigenes, and the Argyraspides to kill Eumenes. Tautamus was initially bribed, but Antigenes changed his mind, and the wider attempt failed when Eumenes answered Antigonus's threatening letter before the soldiers.

l: Alexander's apparition and dream, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: depicts Alexander [appearing alive in royal robes and directing the kingdom] Eumenes dreamed that Alexander appeared in royal robes, seated on his throne and governing the kingdom. He reported the dream as a means of promoting peace and concord, and it led to the creation of the throne and a ceremony honoring Alexander.

l: battle between Eumenes and Antigonus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Eumenes told Olympias to remain in Epirus until the war ended and declared that he would risk himself to preserve the kings. His preparations, recruitment, and planned fleet were directed against Antigonus in the continuing conflict. The text describes preparations for a future battle between Eumenes and Antigonus. Antigonus gathered additional forces after learning that Eumenes had been joined by the provincial governors, but the battle itself is not reported in this unit.

l: Phocion's trial and execution, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_carried_out_by drinking hemlock [according to the custom of the country] Phocion and the others condemned with him were taken to prison and executed by drinking hemlock. Their bodies were cast outside the boundaries of Attica without burial.

l: Eumenes's march into Phoenicia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a military march [undertaken to assemble shipping and establish naval control] After securing the loyalty of the Macedonians and Argyraspides, Eumenes ordered his army to march toward Phoenicia. He intended to gather ships from the coastal cities, command the sea, and transport Polyperchon safely from Macedonia into Asia.

l: history, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The unit presents history as a discipline that should proclaim the truth. It condemns historians who distort the record through personal resentment or gratitude, particularly Timaeus’s attacks on Agathocles and Callias’s excessive praise of him.

l: Alexander, son of Polyperchon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander, son of Polyperchon, is a military commander active in Attica and the Peloponnesus. He came to Attica with an army, seized Munychia and Piraeus for war rather than restoring them, dealt secretly with Nicanor, and received Phocion’s fleeing followers. After allying with Antigonus in Asia, he opposed Cassander, campaigned against Cassander’s garrisons with Aristodemus, then deserted Antigonus for a league with Cassander and command in the Peloponnesus. He took Dyme and was assassinated near Sicyon.

l: Alexander IV, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander IV is Alexander’s son and a young king, brought back into Macedonia with Olympias by Polyperchon and Aeacidas. Cassander later imprisoned him and his mother Roxana at Amphipolis, removed his companions, and ordered that he no longer be treated as a king but as a private person.

l: the garrison, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_stationed_at Munychia [under Nicanor's command] The Athenians initially wanted the garrison to march away as quickly as possible. Nicanor instead reinforced the garrison in Munychia and used it to defend the place and oppose those who might besiege it.

l: the commonalty, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The commonalty had recently been excluded from participation in the government and was restored to its rights. It therefore hated those who had deprived the citizens of their laws and liberties and supported the condemnation of Phocion and his associates, preventing Phocion from being heard.

l: Athenian laws and liberties, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: are_restored_to the Athenians [under the edict restoring Greek liberties] The Athenians appealed to the king, Polyperchon, and Olympias for restoration of their laws and liberties. Their democratic supporters accused Phocion and others of trying to abolish the ancient laws and deprive the citizens of their rights.

l: the Athenian assembly, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: condemns Phocion [to death] The Athenian assembly met after Alexander’s actions and removed the existing magistrates, installed men who favored democracy, and condemned supporters of the oligarchy. It later condemned Phocion and the other accused men to death, although the crowd repeatedly prevented Phocion from presenting an effective defense.

l: Demetrius Phalerius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Demetrius Phalerius is appointed by Cassander president, protector, and guardian of Athens under a peace; he keeps the city peaceful and treats citizens obligingly. After the Piraeus is captured, someone negotiates with him, gains safe conduct, and flees to Thebes and Egypt.

l: the Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Greeks were forces in Africa under Archagathus and his commanders, composed among Agathocles's forces and at war with the Carthaginians. They initially conquered several cities under Eumachus, but at Tunis were hemmed in by land and sea without provisions. After attacking the Carthaginian camp near the river Himera, reinforcements turned the battle against them; many were killed and survivors fled. After Agathocles fled, they received three hundred talents, restored their towns, and either joined the Carthaginians or settled at Selinus.

l: the siege of Megalopolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The siege began when Polyperchon approached Megalopolis with Macedonian and allied forces, long ships, and towers. Megalopolitans resisted by fortifying, rebuilding walls, and disabling elephants, repelling assault; Polyperchon then left part of his army to continue.

l: the naval battle near Byzantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Near Byzantium at sea, Clitus won the first engagement, sinking seventeen enemy ships and capturing at least forty; Antigonus then defeated his fleet through nighttime land and surprise naval attacks.

l: the peace between Athens and Cassander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The peace allowed Athens to retain its city, territory, profits, shipping, and other possessions while becoming Cassander’s friend and ally. Cassander retained Munychia until the war with the kings ended, Athens agreed to pay tribute, and Demetrius the Phalerian became its protector.

l: the battle fought by Agathocles with the Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The battle was fought at a difficult river crossing after the Carthaginians occupied high ground and prepared to resist. Agathocles broke through the opposing battalion and drove the Carthaginians back, while Greek cavalry allied with the Carthaginians fought fiercely. Agathocles then attacked the Carthaginian camp but suffered heavy losses before the Numidians raided his own camp.

l: the fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The fleet was central to the struggle between Cassander, Polyperchon, Clitus, Nicanor, and Antigonus. Clitus initially defeated the opposing fleet, but Antigonus repaired his forces and later captured or destroyed nearly all of Clitus’s ships.

l: oligarchy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_supported_by the Megalopolitans [as their preferred political order] The Megalopolitans favored oligarchy and therefore supported Cassander. Polyperchon’s commissioners were ordered to execute those who had established oligarchic magistrates under Antipater and to restore democratic governments.

l: the tyranny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Agathocles’s tyranny in Syracuse and Sicily is presented as a remarkable overthrow of democracy toward monarchy. Though he sometimes appeared among ordinary people without royal insignia, fear of opposition drove him to rely on mercenaries, massacre suspected enemies, oppress others, and kill relatives.

l: Crotona, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Crotona is a place home to Pythagoreans during Pythagoras’s lifetime, whose Crotonians revered him as a god; Cylo’s rejection by them bred hostility, and Agathocles later deceived, besieged, breached, plundered, and killed its men.

l: Sosistratus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
