s: is_a ruler [successor of Hicetas and ruler of the Syracusans] Sosistratus ruled the Syracusans and controlled Agrigentum and many other cities. He and Thynion sent for Pyrrhus, and Sosistratus later surrendered Agrigentum and its soldiers to him. Pyrrhus reconciled Sosistratus with Thynion and the Syracusans.

l: Dinocrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Dinocrates is a Syracusan leader who serves as captain and general of exiles opposing Agathocles. He revives the Agrigentines’ cause, declares himself Protector of the common liberty, seeks Carthaginian aid, recovers expelled exiles, captures Gabu, and commands large forces and important cities with king-like authority. He repeatedly challenges Agathocles and gains advantages, rejecting an offer because he values his authority and fears becoming a private citizen at Syracuse. Though he prevails in Sicily and Agathocles is willing to resign government, he refuses an arrangement. Desertions weaken his army, which Agathocles routs. Dinocrates is then received into favor, becomes general of part of Agathocles’s army, seizes Pasiphilus at Gela, delivers Gela’s castles and cities to Agathocles, and betrays the confederates.

l: Gela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: recovers political liberty [with Xenodicus's assistance] Agathocles suspected Gela of intending to revolt because the Carthaginian army was encamped in its territory. He secretly filled the city with soldiers, killed about four thousand of its inhabitants, and left a strong garrison there.

l: Morgantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Morgantium is a strong, well-fortified city besieged by Salvius and the rebels. A Roman general's relief attack fails, but the siege ends when the city's slaves fight in its defense.

l: Agathocles's purges, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Agathocles's purges were a campaign against Syracusan and neighboring opponents. He accused the wealthy Syracusan senate of plotting, seized leading men, and ordered killings and plunder. Using an attempted betrayal as pretext, he executed about 600 opponents from Taurominium and Messana and killed Centuripian leaders, leaving Messanians fearful and regretful.

l: the oligarchy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The oligarchy had governed Syracuse through a senate of six hundred before its supporters were expelled from the city. Those favoring an oligarchy later opposed Agathocles, and he used their alleged opposition to justify their destruction and the removal of their influence.

l: Syracusan democracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The democracy was restored or defended in Agathocles's public claims after the exiles returned to Syracuse. He swore that he would not harm it, declared that he would protect it, and used this promise to gain authority before establishing his own absolute command. The Syracusan democracy was restored after Agathocles's death. The Syracusans confiscated Agathocles's goods and estate and broke down his statues.

l: Sicilian exiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Syracusan exiles living in Agrigentum opposed Agathocles and urged war before he grew stronger. They persuaded the Agrigentines to seek a Lacedaemonian general, then gathered under Dinocrates through love of liberty or fear of Agathocles, forming a large, exile-hardened army that challenged him in Sicily.

l: the citizens of Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The citizens of Syracuse were divided by factional disputes and conflict between private individuals. During Agathocles's seizure of power, many were killed or plundered without accusation, while more than six thousand were expelled and many fled to Agrigentum.

l: the soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Soldiers belonging to Agathocles's faction, gathered from Morgantium, inland cities, and veterans of war against the Carthaginians, became enraged after accusations against the six hundred, killed their leaders, plundered opponents, and carried out the massacre at Syracuse.

l: the massacre at Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: creates more than six thousand exiles [expelled from Syracuse] The massacre began when Agathocles ordered his soldiers to attack the leaders of the six hundred and seize their property. The violence spread throughout the city, killing more than four thousand people in one day and driving more than six thousand into exile, while houses, streets, and even temples became scenes of violence.

l: Agathocles's seizure of power, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Agathocles's seizure of power was prepared by raising an army under the pretext of suppressing an insurrection at Erbita. He arrested leading men of the six hundred, provoked his soldiers to massacre and plunder their opponents, and then persuaded the assembly to appoint him sole general with full and absolute authority.

l: the Carthaginian war against Agathocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Carthaginians intensified war against Agathocles as his power spread through Sicily. After a destructive storm, Amilcar rebuilt their forces, defeated him, and gained cities. Four years of hardship ended when Agathocles’s remaining soldiers made peace, restoring Carthaginian peace and liberty.

l: the Roman-Samnite War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Roman-Samnite War was a war between Romans and Samnites for sovereignty over Italy. It unfolded through raids, sieges, and battles at Ferentum, Saticula, and Lautulae; despite a serious Roman defeat at Lautulae, successes under Quintus Fabius and colonies at Luceria and Pontia strengthened Roman attacks and gains.

l: Eudamus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Eudamus comes from India with five hundred horse, three thousand foot, and elephants obtained by treacherously killing Porus after Alexander's death; Eumenes pays him to secure his allegiance and elephants.

l: Polemon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Polemon, sent by Antigonus to free Greek cities, acts for him in Greece and becomes Athens’ chief magistrate the next year.

l: Macedonian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Macedonian army under Eumenes was endangered when Seleucus and Python flooded its camp near the Tigris. It crossed the river in flat-bottomed boats and later marched through Susiana in three divisions because provisions were scarce.

l: king's pavilion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: contains Alexander's throne [used as the army's council place] The king's pavilion contained Alexander's throne and had been used for incense offerings and deliberations on important affairs. Eumenes proposed that the commanders meet there daily to govern collectively, and the assembled leaders accepted the arrangement.

l: Macedonian succession crisis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a revolution in the state [anticipated after Olympias's conduct in Macedonia] The Macedonian succession crisis is reflected in the struggle among Olympias, Eurydice, Philip III Arrhidaeus, Cassander, and Polyperchon for control of Macedonia. Olympias's seizure of power and subsequent executions provoked opposition and were said to point clearly toward a revolution in the state.

l: Ceteus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Ceteus, commander of Indians, led soldiers from India in battle, fought with great resolution, and was killed, leaving two wives who had accompanied him during the campaign.

l: Peucestes's feast, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Peucestes's feast was a four-round gathering for the army and leaders, its largest circle ten furlongs around. Mercenaries and allies, Macedonian silver targeteers, officers, horsemen, generals, Persian nobility, and altars filled the circles. It won soldiers' favor but made Eumenes suspect Peucestes sought supreme command.

l: Antigonus's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antigonus's army was a large, mixed military force of infantry, cavalry, elephants, and troops from several regions. It approached Eumenes's army but was delayed by a river, trench, and bad ground, skirmishing and foraging before pursuit; it later numbered over 28,000 foot, 8,500 horse, and 65 elephants. Though its left wing and phalanx were routed, remaining forces counterattacked, rallied, buried the dead, and marched to provisioned Gamarga. It then marched via Babylon, captured Gaza and Joppa, besieged Tyre, built a fleet, and finally turned back toward Syria after hardship in the desert toward Egypt.

l: Gabene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Gabene, a country three days’ march from the armies, is identified by Eumenes as Antigonus’s objective; untouched and rich in corn and forage, it can supply a large army and is defended by rivers and deep ravines.

l: battle, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Battle: approaching armies initially cannot engage because a river, deep trench, and difficult ground divide them; after movements and deceptions, both form up as commanders unusually arrange their forces.

l: march to Gabene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a military movement [intended to secure provisions and advantageous ground] The march to Gabene was pursued by both sides because the region offered abundant provisions and strong defensive terrain. Eumenes sent a false warning of a night attack, causing Antigonus to halt temporarily, while Eumenes's army moved ahead. Antigonus later resumed the march and pursued Eumenes toward Gabene.

l: stratagem, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Eumenes used hired mercenaries disguised as deserters to make Antigonus believe that a night attack was imminent. Antigonus and Eumenes then each tried to deceive the other about the position and strength of their forces, showing that both generals relied heavily on stratagems rather than direct action alone.

l: the enemy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The enemy's strength was arranged in cavalry, infantry, elephants, and a phalanx. Its troops were attacked by Python's horsemen, later routed by Eumenes's infantry and the Argyraspides, and then partly rallied and counterattacked under Antigonus.

l: the battle, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The battle near the mountains involved Antigonus and Eumenes, from initial cavalry and infantry charges through Eumenes's early gains and Antigonus's counterattack. Both armies prepared to resume fighting at night, then encamped; it ended with casualties and burial rights sought.

l: the funeral of Ceteus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: At Ceteus’s funeral, a pyre was prepared and his two wives competed to die with him. Captains selected the younger after midwives found the elder pregnant; she proceeded ceremonially to self-immolation.

l: the dead soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The dead soldiers lay at the original battlefield after the armies had withdrawn. Eumenes wanted to return and bury his dead as a sign of victory, while Antigonus encamped near the bodies, obtained the privilege of burying them, and used that fact to claim an appearance of victory.

l: the funeral pyre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The funeral pyre was prepared for Ceteus, and the younger wife was placed upon it by her brother. Before it was kindled, the army marched three times around it; she then died without showing fear of the flames.

l: the battle's casualties, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antigonus's side lost three thousand seven hundred infantry and fifty-four horsemen, with more than four thousand wounded. Eumenes's side lost five hundred and forty infantry and very few horsemen, with more than nine hundred wounded.

l: Epirots, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Epirots are a people willing to fight for their country and allies. Ruled for a time by Alcetas, they killed him after his rule became severe and tyrannical. They later mutinied, banished Aeacidas, allied with Cassander, were routed, made Alcetas king, and suffered further defeats.

l: Perrhaebia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Polyperchon was stationed in Perrhaebia with his army. Cassander sent Callas against him and sent Dinias to secure the passes, which were occupied before Olympias's forces could arrive.

l: revolt of the Epirotes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Epirotes sent back to their country revolted against Aeacidas. By a common decree, the state banished him from the kingdom and allied with Cassander, an action described as unprecedented in Epirus since the reign of Neoptolemus.

l: battle between Antigonus and Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antigonus and Eumenes fought after encamping near each other: Antigonus's horse prevailed and captured Eumenes's baggage, but Eumenes's Argyraspides defeated the opposing infantry, killing over five thousand without losses.

l: capture of Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_caused_by Macedonians [after they secretly corresponded with Antigonus] After the battle, the Macedonians secretly corresponded with Antigonus and seized Eumenes. They delivered him to Antigonus in exchange for their carriages and security, then marched away with the rest of the army.

l: execution of Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_ordered_by Antigonus [under pressure from the Macedonians] Antigonus initially imprisoned Eumenes and considered employing him because he valued him as a general. At the pressing requests of the Macedonians, however, Antigonus put Eumenes to death and had his body burned, placing his bones in an urn for his nearest friends.

l: Antigonus's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: has_strength 22,000 foot, 9,000 horse, and 65 elephants [excluding troops listed in Media] Antigonus's army marched through a barren desert with ten days of provisions and attempted to conceal its fires at night. It later numbered twenty-two thousand foot, nine thousand horse, and sixty-five elephants, not counting forces listed in Media.

l: fire-signal stratagem, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Eumenes ordered fires to be lit at posts spread across high ground so that they appeared to show an army encamped near the wilderness. The deception caused Antigonus to halt and turn aside, giving Eumenes time to assemble his forces and fortify his camp.

l: flood near Rhodes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: An inundation near the city of Rhodes followed violent spring storms, rain, and large hailstones, flooded lower areas, killed over five hundred people, damaged houses, and drained through a wall breach.

l: Python's conspiracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Python’s conspiracy won over soldiers in winter quarters and caused an army defection; after Python’s execution, supporters raised eight hundred horse, fought in Media, and were killed or captured.

l: treasure of Susa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: includes golden vine [among other rarities] The treasure of Susa included a golden vine and other rarities valued at fifteen thousand talents. Along with crowns, presents, spoils, and additional treasure from Media, it contributed to Antigonus’s total accumulation of twenty-five thousand talents.

l: Cassandria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cassandria, founded and named by Cassander in Pallene, was populated with people from the Chersonesus, Potidaea, neighbouring cities, and surviving Olynthians. Given a large territory, it rapidly grew to become Macedonia's most powerful city.

l: rebuilding of Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cassander undertakes rebuilding Thebes for fame and honor, restoring its renowned city with walls built largely by Athenians and aid from Greek communities, Sicily, and Italy.

l: siege of Pydna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The siege of Pydna, commanded by Cassander, lasted from winter into spring; he blocked land and sea relief, causing famine until the besieged abandoned the city or surrendered.

l: famine at Pydna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The famine at Pydna became extreme: tiny bread rations led to sawdust-fed elephants, slaughtered animals, deaths among foreign horsemen and others, cannibalism by some barbarians, and a city filled with unburied corpses.

l: Cinna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cinna allies with Gaius Marius during the Roman civil conflict, agrees to peace, and is restored to the consulship as Lucius Cornelius Merula surrenders it.

l: Macedonian expedition into Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: has_target Peloponnesus Cassander raised Macedonian soldiers and marched toward Peloponnesus to drive out Alexander, the son of Polyperchon. After finding the isthmus strongly guarded, he moved through Megara, transported his elephants and army to Epidaurus, secured Argos and Messenia, and then returned to Macedonia after leaving two thousand men near the isthmus.

l: Polyclitus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Polyclitus, Seleucus’s lieutenant and fleet commander, commands Ptolemy’s hundred ships to Cyprus, defeats Antigonus’s forces near Cilicia, captures leaders and ships, then returns via Cyprus to Pelusium for reward.

l: Menelaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Ptolemy's chief commander in Cyprus and governor of Salamis, Menelaus led forces against Demetrius, was routed, defended the city by burning siege engines, and lost Salamis after Ptolemy's defeat.

l: Ptolemy's fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: has_size one hundred ships [quick sailers from Egypt] Ptolemy's fleet included a hundred swift and well-equipped ships sent from Egypt under Seleucus. It sailed past Antigonus's camp near Tyre and demonstrated that Ptolemy's side controlled the sea at that time.

l: ships, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Antigonus initially had almost no ships, so he ordered the rulers of Phoenicia and Syria to build them and established several arsenals. His newly built navy, together with ships from Rhodes and the Hellespont, eventually totaled two hundred and forty warships, which he divided between the Peloponnesus and Dioscorides.

l: Tyre siege, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a siege [conducted by Antigonus against Tyre] The Tyre siege lasted thirteen months. Antigonus's naval blockade prevented supplies from reaching the city, and Tyre surrendered after its inhabitants were reduced to great distress.

l: Antigonus's war against the four kings, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Ptolemy, Cassander, and Lysimachus prepared a war against Antigonus after he refused their demands. Their forces operated through Egypt, Cyprus, Caria, Cappadocia, and the Peloponnesus, while Antigonus sought additional allies and built a fleet. Antigonus's war against Ptolemy Lagus, Seleucus, Lysimachus, and Cassander ended with Antigonus's death in battle. Demetrius and Stratonice then fled with their wealth to Cyprus.

l: league against Antigonus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Ptolemy, Cassander, and Lysimachus entered into a league against Antigonus after their embassy to him failed. They gathered forces, obtained arms and supplies, and coordinated operations against his supporters.

l: Prepelaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cassander's general who lost Corinth to Demetrius and returned, then led forces in Asia, captured Adramyttium, helped secure Ephesus, and won Teos and Colophon.

l: Dymæans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Dymaeans rebel against Cassander’s garrison, wall off their city and besiege the citadel; Alexander defeats them, but Aristodemus’s mercenaries help them retake it and kill Alexander’s supporters.

l: Acrotatus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a son of Cleomenes [Lacedaemonian nobleman] Acrotatus, son of King Cleomenes, accepted command of the forces opposing Agathocles and sailed for Agrigentum. He became cruel and luxurious, mismanaged and robbed the treasury, murdered Sosistratus, was deposed and nearly stoned, and fled back to Laconia.

l: Amilcar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Amilcar is a Carthaginian commander and general whose records center on campaigns in Sicily and Spain and on the enlargement of Carthaginian power. Against Agathocles, he rebuilt his army in Sicily, defeated him at the river Himera, won several Sicilian cities, and marched on Syracuse. He tried to seize its walls, later besieged it by cutting supplies, but a night defeat led to his capture, torture, and killing by Syracusans; his head was sent to Agathocles. Other records place him in Sicily after Hanno the elder, defeating Romans at Thermæ, gaining places, fortifying Drepanum, and destroying Eryx except its temple area. He then advanced toward the Pillars of Hercules and Gades, subdued Iberians, Tartessians, and Celts, founded Acra Leuca, and gained many Spanish cities. His career ends in another account with drowning while fleeing across a river after raising the siege of Helice. He is regarded as among the greatest captains, with victories that greatly enlarged Carthaginian dominions.

l: Agathocles' war with the Sicilian Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Agathocles fought the Messenians and attempted to seize Messina, but the Messenians resisted with help from exiles. The Agrigentines, Geloans, and Messenians later made peace with him through Carthaginian mediation, after which he subdued several Greek cities in Sicily.

l: Greek cities of Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Greek cities of Sicily opposed or submitted to Agathocles at different times. Heraclea, Selinus, and Himera were assigned to Carthage by treaty, while the other cities under Syracusan power were declared free before Agathocles later brought many of them under his control.

l: cities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_in_revolt revolt [several cities] Several cities revolt, and Lysimachus comes against them. Antigonus gains the cities in Caria, while Polemon is sent into Greece to set the cities at liberty.

l: Italians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Italians rebelled against Rome after repeated promises of citizenship were not fulfilled. They organized a rival government, divided Italy between their consuls, and called their new city Italy. After suffering repeated defeats and losing allies, they abandoned the city and moved to Aesernia.

l: Athenaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Athenaeus is a commander sent by Antigonus with infantry and cavalry to raid the Nabataeans. He captures their stronghold, kills or imprisons defenders, and takes valuable plunder, but returning Arabians destroy his exhausted, unwatched army.

l: Nabataeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Nabataeans are an Arabian people who value liberty and live as solitary nomads in the desert. They protect cattle, families, wealth, and trade goods by using separate desert refuges, watch-towers, scouts, and a strong rock. After Athenaeus captures their rock and takes myrrh, frankincense, and silver, they pursue and destroy his army. They then complain to Antigonus, resist Demetrius’s invasion, and secure peace by giving gifts and hostages.
